blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A study design is the plan that decides which units are studied, how they are selected, and when exposure and outcome are measured. An exposure is a factor whose effect or association you study (e.g. not being exclusively breastfed); an outcome is the event or condition you measure (e.g. diarrhoea). Descriptive designs (case report, case series, cross-sectional survey) describe how much disease there is and in whom. Analytical designs compare groups to study an exposure–outcome association: ecological, case-control, cohort and the randomised controlled trial (RCT). Hybrid designs sample from within a cohort: the nested case-control study and the case-cohort study.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
The design decides which numbers the data can give you. Four measures recur:

  • Prevalence: the proportion of a population that has the condition at one time (existing cases ÷ population).
  • Risk (incidence proportion): the proportion of initially disease-free people who develop the condition over a stated period (new cases ÷ people at risk at the start).
  • Rate (incidence rate): new cases per unit of person-time (the time each person was observed while at risk, added up), e.g. per 1,000 child-years (§7.4 treats rates fully).
  • Odds: the probability of an event divided by the probability of it not happening, p ÷ (1 − p) (used for 2 × 2 tables in §10.6.4).

A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at the same moment, so it gives prevalence, but it cannot tell which came first. A cohort study starts with disease-free people, classifies them by exposure, and follows them forward (or, in a retrospective cohort, through past records) to count new cases, so it gives risk and rate. A case-control study starts from the outcome: it selects people with the disease (cases) and without it (controls) and looks back for past exposure. The investigator fixes how many cases and controls there are, so the study cannot estimate prevalence or risk; it compares the odds of exposure between cases and controls. An RCT is a cohort in which the investigator assigns the exposure at random, which balances other factors between groups on average (§15.9). An ecological study uses groups (villages, districts) as units, relating a group’s exposure level to its disease rate.

The hybrid designs save money inside a large cohort. A nested case-control study takes every case that arises in the cohort and, for each, samples controls from cohort members still at risk at that time. A case-cohort study takes a random subcohort at the start and adds all cases; the same subcohort serves as the comparison group for every outcome.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Design Unit Sampled on Can estimate Analysed in
Case series Individuals (cases only) Outcome Counts and features of cases; no rate Chapters 2–4 (description)
Cross-sectional Individuals Neither (a population sample) Prevalence; prevalence ratio or odds ratio §7.2, §10.6, §13.7
Ecological Groups Group Group rates and their correlation §11.2, Chapter 12
Case-control Individuals Outcome Odds ratio of exposure §10.6.4, §10.8, §13.2
Cohort Individuals Exposure (or a population, then classified) Risk, rate, risk ratio, rate ratio, hazard ratio (a ratio of instantaneous event rates, Chapter 14) §7.4, §10.6.4, §13.5, Chapter 14
RCT Individuals (or clusters) Assigned exposure Risk or rate in each arm; effect of the assigned intervention §15.9
Nested case-control / case-cohort Individuals within a cohort Outcome, within the cohort The full cohort’s ratio measures (e.g. rate or hazard ratio), with exposure measured on far fewer people §13.2.9, Chapter 14

The ecological trap is real. Robinson (1950) found that the correlation between illiteracy and the proportion of Black residents was 0.77 across the 48 US states but only 0.20 across individuals. Group-level association cannot be read as individual-level association: the ecological fallacy.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
A district has 10,000 children, of whom 100 (1%) had dysentery this season. An investigator runs a case-control study: all 100 cases and 200 controls.

  1. Proportion with dysentery among the 300 studied = 100 ÷ 300 = 33.3%.
  2. True proportion affected in the district = 100 ÷ 10,000 = 1.0%.
  3. Had she chosen 400 controls, the study proportion would be 100 ÷ 500 = 20.0%, with the district unchanged.

Result: in a case-control study the “proportion diseased” (33.3% or 20.0%) is set by the investigator’s control-to-case ratio. It says nothing about prevalence or risk, which is why case-control studies report odds ratios of exposure instead.

blocks.label: Common Misreading
blocks.html: “The design with the most statistical machinery gives the strongest evidence.” The analysis must match the design, not the other way round. A logistic regression on a cross-sectional survey still cannot tell whether exposure came before outcome; a perfectly analysed ecological correlation still cannot be applied to individuals.

points.html: Descriptive designs generate hypotheses; analytical designs test associations. Only the RCT assigns exposure, so only it balances unmeasured factors between groups, on average, by design.
Case-control: sampled on outcome; efficient for rare diseases; gives an odds ratio of exposure, not prevalence or risk.
Cohort: sampled on exposure or as a population; gives risk and rate; efficient for rare exposures; needs follow-up.
Cross-sectional: gives prevalence; exposure and outcome measured together, so temporality is often unknown.
Ecological: the unit is a group; beware the ecological fallacy (Robinson, 1950).
§8.8 extends this map into a table of design × outcome type → test or model.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 1.6

questions.prompt: A resident surveys 400 randomly chosen women in a block on one day, recording current tobacco use and current hypertension. Name the design and the measure of disease frequency it can give. Why can it not show that tobacco use preceded hypertension?
questions.answer: Cross-sectional survey; it gives the prevalence of hypertension (and of tobacco use) at that time. Exposure and outcome are measured at the same moment, so the survey cannot show which came first; a woman might, for example, have changed her tobacco use after being told she had hypertension.

questions.prompt: A case-control study of 80 neonatal tetanus cases uses 240 controls. What proportion of the study sample are cases? Why is this not the incidence of neonatal tetanus?
questions.answer: Proportion = 80 ÷ (80 + 240) = 80 ÷ 320 = 25%. The investigator chose 3 controls per case; with 1 control per case the figure would be 50%. The proportion reflects the sampling ratio, not the number of new cases among all births, so it estimates neither incidence nor prevalence.

questions.prompt: Districts with more mobile phones per household have lower infant mortality. Name the design and the error of concluding that a mother’s phone lowers her own infant’s risk of death.
questions.answer: Ecological study (units are districts). Concluding an individual-level effect from a group-level association is the ecological fallacy: district phone ownership may simply mark wealth, roads and facilities, and within districts the infants who died may have had phones as often as those who survived.
